questions_and_answers.question: Which pair illustrates the difference between a long and a short vowel?
According to the notes, what is true about the German diphthong as in 'Wein'?

answers.answer: Its duration is shorter than the English vowel combination
It lasts longer than the English vowel combination
It is the same length as the English vowel combination
It always ends with an r sound

questions_and_answers.question: What is said about post-vocalic r in German?

answers.answer: It has a vowel-like sound and does not sound like the English r
It is identical to the English r

questions_and_answers.question: What observation is made about syllables containing post-vocalic r?

answers.answer: They are slightly longer than syllables without it
They are shorter than syllables without it

questions_and_answers.question: Which pair belongs to Practice 3 for post-vocalic r?
How is the pre-vocalic ch pronounced according to the notes?

answers.answer: With slight friction between the back of the tongue and the soft palate, similar to the final sound in durch and nach
With the front of the tongue against the teeth

questions_and_answers.question: Which list of words is used to practise the pre-vocalic ch sound (Practice 5)?
What method does the notes suggest for pronouncing words with pre-vocalic ch after consonants?

answers.answer: Whisper an extra syllable at the beginning if necessary

questions_and_answers.question: Which pair is used to practise long versus short vowels with post-vocalic r?
Which example is given to illustrate the German diphthong practise?

articles.text:
Notes on Pronunciation
A. Long and short vowels.
Practice 1:
ihn - in
Beet - Bett
Staat - Stadt
bog - Bock
bieten - bitten
beten - Betten
wate - Watte
wohne - Wonne
Lied - litt
den - denn
Wahn - wann
lohte - Lotte
mieten - mitten
Sehne - Senne
bahne - banne
Ofen - offen
Mus - musa
König - können
Hüte - Hütte
Pute - Putte
Höhle - Hölle
fühle - fülle
bucht - Bucht
böge - Böcke
müder - Mutter
Muhme - Mume
Goethe - Götter
Lüge - Lücke

B. Diphthongs.
Ask your instructor to say German Wein, then say English "wine". Notice that the duration of the German vowel combination is considerably shorter than the English.
Practice 2:
mein
Wein
nein
leider

C. Post-vocalic r.
Haus
Maus
auch
glaube
neu
neun
deutsch
Leute
Post-vocalic r in German has a vowel-like sound. It does not sound like the English r. Listen carefully to the following pairs of words and imitate them to the satisfaction of your instructor.
Practice 3:
diese - dieser
Miete - Mieter
älter - Eltern
Gästen - gestern
eine - einer
Alte - Alter
Vetter - Vettern
locken - lockern
Liebe - lieber
bitte - bitter
Kinder - Kindern
fetten - Vettern
Ode - oder
welche - welcher
Note that the syllable with post-vocalic r is in every case slightly longer than the syllable without it. If you watch your instructor's lips carefully you may also see that they are slightly farther apart, his mouth slightly more open on this syllable.
Now practice the following groups, first the long vowels and then the pairs of long and short vowels with post-vocalic r, and finally the vowels followed by r and a consonant.
Practice 4:
hier
sehr
Uhr
Ohr
her - Herr
Bier
mehr
fuhr
Tor
wir - wirr
wir
her
nur
Mohr
Star - starr
Mark
dort
Herrn
Furt
Wirt
Park
Dorf
gern
Durst
First
darf
Wort
herb
Wurm
Schirm
hart
Kork
Kerl
Kurve
Birne

D. Pre-vocalic ch (voiceless).
The pre-vocalic ch differs from the post-vocalic ch. Most speakers of German make the pre-vocalic ch with slight friction between the back of the tongue and the soft palate, the region back of the mouth near the uvula. This sound is very similar to the final sound in durch and nach.
Practice the following groups:
Practice 5:
noch
doch
nach
auch
lachen
pochen
tauchen
Dachau
Bochum
Bucholz
Now try making the same sound right after the initial consonants in the following groups:
Practice 6:
Frau
fragen
froh
Trost
traute
treffen
Prost
prall
Preis
Krone
Kragen
krumm
Do you understand mich?
Yes, ich verstehe you well.
How goes it with regard to you? (How are you?)
He speaks English with r.
You may find it necessary at first to whisper an extra syllable at the beginning of these words and pronounce Fochau, Tochost, pochall, Kochone, etc. Don't hesitate to try this if necessary.
